key_facts: Excessive, symmetrical sweating of the armpits, palms, soles or face that interferes with daily life.
Overactive cholinergic sympathetic signalling to normal eccrine glands (primary), or a systemic cause (secondary).
Exclude secondary causes; aluminium chloride at night; tap-water iontophoresis for hands and feet; specialist botulinum toxin or oral anticholinergics.
Secondary causes: thyrotoxicosis, infection (TB), lymphoma, menopause, drugs (SSRIs), phaeochromocytoma.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Sweating beyond what is needed for thermoregulation.

ul: **Primary focal hyperhidrosis:** idiopathic; axillae, palms, soles, craniofacial; affects ~1–3% of people.
**Secondary hyperhidrosis:** generalised (or focal from neurological lesions), due to a medical condition or drug.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Primary: overactivity of the sympathetic cholinergic supply to normal eccrine glands (central dysregulation; family history in ~30–50%). Secondary: increased metabolic rate (thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma), hormonal change (**hypogonadism**, menopause), infection/malignancy (cytokines), drugs, **obesity** (insulation, higher metabolic demand), **obstructive sleep apnoea**, autonomic/neurological disease.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: The case: a **41-year-old man**, sweating **"at the drop of a hat", at most times of day**, **forehead and axillae**, **deteriorating over 1 year**, potent antiperspirants ineffective, **BMI 34**; FBC/LFT/TFT/HbA1c normal.

head: Primary focal
Secondary
rows: Weight change, fever, flushing, palpitations, sexual dysfunction, snoring

blocks: **Primary focal criteria (Hornberger 2004):** focal, visible, excessive sweating for **≥6 months** without an apparent cause, plus **≥2** of: bilateral and relatively symmetrical; impairs daily activities; **≥1 episode/week**; **onset <25 years**; **family history**; **stops during sleep**. This man meets few of them (onset at 40, 1-year history), so **secondary hyperhidrosis must be excluded** — the answer to the course question.

ul: **Further history:** **Drugs:** SSRIs/SNRIs (sertraline, venlafaxine, duloxetine), TCAs, opioids (incl. methadone), insulin/sulfonylureas (hypoglycaemia), pilocarpine/cholinesterase inhibitors, antipyretics, GnRH analogues, tamoxifen/aromatase inhibitors, **testosterone withdrawal/anabolic steroids**, PPIs, prostaglandin analogues; **Alcohol** (and withdrawal); **recreational drugs — cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA** (course teaching: often not asked); caffeine; nicotine; **Hypogonadism symptoms:** erectile dysfunction, low libido, **reduced shaving frequency**, fatigue, low mood, gynaecomastia; **Acromegaly:** ring/shoe size change, coarse features, headaches, snoring; **OSA:** snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness (STOP-BANG, Epworth); **Phaeochromocytoma:** paroxysmal headache, palpitations, pallor, hypertension; **Infection/malignancy:** fever, **night sweats**, weight loss, lymph nodes, TB exposure/travel, HIV risk; **Carcinoid:** flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze; GORD (nocturnal sweats); anxiety/social phobia; heart failure; neurological (Parkinson's, spinal cord injury, stroke); hypoglycaemic episodes; **Impact:** HDSS (Hyperhidrosis Disease Severity Scale, 1–4), DLQI, mood

**Investigations** beyond those done: **9 am fasting total testosterone** (repeat if low) with **SHBG, LH/FSH** and **prolactin**; **fasting glucose/lipids** (metabolic); **urine drug screen** (with consent); **plasma free or 24-h urinary metanephrines** if paroxysmal/hypertensive; **IGF-1** if acromegalic features; **ESR/CRP, HIV test, CXR** (TB/lymphoma) if systemic features; **24-h urinary 5-HIAA** if flushing/diarrhoea; **sleep study** if OSA likely; BP, ECG; the starch–iodine (Minor) test to map focal areas (specialist)

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: Primary focal hyperhidrosis; obesity-related sweating; **male hypogonadism** (obesity-related functional hypogonadism); OSA; drugs/alcohol/cocaine; thyrotoxicosis (TFT normal); diabetes/hypoglycaemia (HbA1c normal, but ask about sulfonylureas/insulin); phaeochromocytoma; acromegaly; carcinoid; lymphoma/TB/HIV/endocarditis; anxiety; gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome, diabetes); compensatory hyperhidrosis (after sympathectomy).

sections.title: Management

ul: **Treat the cause.** Weight loss (NICE obesity pathways; GLP-1/GIP agonists where eligible), alcohol/cocaine cessation support, CPAP for OSA, endocrine referral for hypogonadism (testosterone replacement is specialist-guided and usually reserved for confirmed organic hypogonadism or persistent symptoms after weight loss), drug switches (e.g. a different SSRI, or a dose reduction).

**Symptomatic (CKS/BAD stepwise):** Lifestyle: loose natural fibres, avoid triggers (spicy food, alcohol, caffeine), dress shields; **Aluminium chloride hexahydrate 20%** (e.g. Driclor) applied **at night to dry skin**, washed off in the morning; nightly until controlled, then 1–2×/week. If it irritates, use less often or apply hydrocortisone 1%; do not use on broken or recently shaved skin; **Tap-water iontophoresis** (palms/soles; also axillae) — secondary care or home devices; **Botulinum toxin A** intradermal injections (licensed for severe axillary hyperhidrosis; lasts 4–9 months); **Oral anticholinergics:** **propantheline bromide** 15 mg three times daily (licensed for hyperhidrosis); **oxybutynin** or **glycopyrronium** (off-label, specialist). Anticholinergic burden matters — dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, glaucoma, cognitive effects in older people; **Microwave thermolysis** (miraDry — NICE IPG601) and **endoscopic thoracic sympathectomy** (NICE IPG487 — compensatory sweating is common) for severe refractory disease

blocks: History/drug review, first-line tests, aluminium chloride and propantheline prescribing within competence, deprescribing/switching culprits, lifestyle support, and referral for endocrine/specialist treatments.

refer.t: Generalised or night sweats with weight loss, fever or lymph nodes: look for **TB, lymphoma or other systemic disease**.
One-sided or new-onset sweating in later life: consider a neurological cause.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Generalised or night sweats with weight loss, fever or lymph nodes: look for **TB, lymphoma or other systemic disease**.
One-sided or new-onset sweating in later life: consider a neurological cause.

blocks: Night sweats, weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy (lymphoma/TB — urgent); paroxysmal headache/palpitations/hypertension (phaeochromocytoma); unilateral or asymmetric sweating (neurological — e.g. Pancoast tumour, stroke); new onset after 40 without an explanation; acromegalic features; symptoms of hypogonadism.

pearls: "**New sweating at 40 is secondary until proven otherwise**" — ask about drugs, cocaine, alcohol, sleep, sex and weight.
Aluminium chloride works only on **dry skin at night**, when sweat glands are least active.
Many SSRIs and venlafaxine cause dose-related sweating. Switching or reducing the dose often helps; the evidence for adding an anticholinergic is limited.
